claim: Sox2 and Bra are co-expressed in nuclei of all PZ cells in quail embryos at stages HH10-11.
source: As expected, analyses of immunodetection experiments revealed co-expression of Sox2 and Bra in nuclei of all PZ cells (Figure 1A–C) (n=8 embryos).
evidence: Supported by immunodetection experiments performed on 8 embryos at stages HH10-11.

claim: There is high heterogeneity in the relative levels of Sox2 and Bra proteins between neighboring PZ cells.
source: Noticeably, we observed a high heterogeneity in the relative levels of Sox2 and Bra proteins between neighboring PZ cells.
evidence: Observed through immunodetection experiments and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: PZ cells display intermingled cells with high Sox2 and low Bra levels, high Bra and low Sox2 levels, and cells with equivalent levels of both proteins.
source: We indeed found intermingled cells displaying high Sox2 (Sox2high) and low Bra (Bralow) levels and, conversely, Brahigh and Sox2low levels as well as cells in which both proteins appear to be at equivalent levels.
evidence: Observed through immunodetection experiments and cellular-level analysis shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Sox2 and Bra protein levels are very homogenous between neighboring cells in the adjacent nascent tissues (NT and PSM).
source: This cellular heterogeneity was very apparent when compared to the adjacent nascent tissues, that is, the NT and the PSM, where Sox2 and Bra protein levels were found to be very homogenous between neighboring cells (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Observed through immunodetection experiments comparing PZ to NT and PSM tissues.

claim: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity in posterior progenitors is detected as early as stages HH5-6.
source: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity in posterior progenitor was detected as early as stages HH5–6, a stage corresponding to initial activation of Sox2 and Bra co-expression in the quail embryo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through immunodetection experiments at early developmental stages.

claim: Heterogeneous levels of Sox2 and Bra proteins are observed in PZ cells of chicken embryos.
source: We also observed heterogeneous levels of Sox2 and Bra proteins in PZ cells of chicken embryo, indicating that it is not a specific feature of quail (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed through immunodetection experiments in chicken embryos.

claim: Along the neural path, the average expression level of Sox2 increases (+2.22 folds) while that of Bra decreases (−3.81 folds).
source: Data showed that the average expression level of Sox2 increases (+2.22 folds, n=7 embryos) while that of Bra decreases (−3.81 folds) following the neural path (Figure 1G).
evidence: Quantified from immunodetection data across 7 embryos along putative neural trajectories.

claim: Along the paraxial mesoderm path, the average expression level of Sox2 decreases (−2.12 folds) while Bra level first increases in the posterior PSM (1.14 folds) and decreases anteriorly (−5.06 folds).
source: On the contrary, along the paraxial mesoderm path, the average expression level of Sox2 decreases (−2.12 folds, n=7 embryos) while Bra level first increases in the posterior PSM (1.14 folds, positions 1–2) and decreases anteriorly (−5.06 folds, positions 2–7) (Figure 1G').
evidence: Quantified from immunodetection data across 7 embryos along putative PSM trajectories.

claim: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the PZ is preferentially driven by differences in Sox2 levels (coefficient of variation of 41.8%) compared to Bra levels (coefficient of variation of 30.75%).
source: By plotting Sox2 and Bra levels in individual cells, we noticed a broader distribution for Sox2 levels (coefficient of variation of 41.8%) compared to Bra levels (coefficient of variation of 30.75%) (Figure 1H), indicating that the cell-to-cell heterogeneity in the PZ is preferentially driven by differences in Sox2 levels.
evidence: Quantified from single-cell protein level measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Cells with a low Sox2/Bra ratio are more represented in the most posterior part of the PZ.
source: cells with a low ratio level (BraHigh Sox2Low) were found to be more represented in the most posterior part of the PZ (Figure 1J''').
evidence: Observed through spatial distribution analysis of Sox2/Bra ratios on optical sections.

claim: Variations of Sox2/Bra values are present in all areas of the PZ, indicating that Sox2/Bra-related cell-to-cell heterogeneity is present in the whole PZ.
source: However, it should be noted that variations of Sox2/Bra values were noticed in all these areas, indicating that the Sox2/Bra-related cell-to-cell heterogeneity is present in the whole PZ.
evidence: Observed through spatial distribution analysis across different regions of the PZ.

claim: Overexpression of Bra leads to a significant decrease in the Sox2/Bra ratio in PZ cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the Sox2/Bra levels by either overexpressing Bra or downregulating Sox2 and a significant increase of this ratio when Sox2 was overexpressed or when Bra was downregulated (Figure 2A,F).
evidence: Measured 7 hours after electroporation through immunodetection experiments.

claim: Overexpression of Sox2 leads to a significant increase in the Sox2/Bra ratio in PZ cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the Sox2/Bra levels by either overexpressing Bra or downregulating Sox2 and a significant increase of this ratio when Sox2 was overexpressed or when Bra was downregulated (Figure 2A,F).
evidence: Measured 7 hours after electroporation through immunodetection experiments.

claim: Overexpression of Bra leads to a marked reduction of fluorescent signal in the PZ (1.17±0.57%) and an increased signal in the PSM (33.04±4.06%).
source: We next found that overexpression of Bra leads to a marked reduction of the fluorescent signal in the PZ (1.17±0.57%) and to an increased signal in the PSM (33.04±4.06%) but has no effect on the NT signal (Figure 2B,C,E).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence distribution in electroporated embryos at stages HH10-11.

claim: Overexpression of Sox2 drives exit of cells from the PZ (1.16±0.67%) and favors their localization in the NT (75.40±4.57%).
source: Similarly, we found that overexpression of Sox2 drives exit of the cells from the PZ (1.16±0.67%) favoring their localization in the NT (75.40±4.57%) without significantly affecting proportions of cells in the PSM (Figure 2B,D,E).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence distribution in electroporated embryos at stages HH10-11.

claim: Downregulation of Bra leads to exit of cells from the PZ (4.16±1.57%) and favors cell localization in the NT (88.23±2.04%) at the expense of the PSM (7.59±1.81%).
source: We found that downregulation of Bra leads to exit of cells from the PZ (4.16±1.57%) and favors cell localization in the NT (88.23±2.04%) at the expense of the PSM (7.59±1.81%) (Figure 2G,H,J).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence distribution in morpholino-electroporated embryos at stages HH10-11.

claim: Sox2 downregulation triggers cell exit from the PZ (7.50±2.35%) and leads to higher contribution of cells to the PSM (34.59±4.79%).
source: Similarly, Sox2 downregulation triggers cell exit from the PZ (7.50±2.35%) and, as expected, leads to higher contribution of cells to the PSM (34.59±4.79%) but this does not occur at the expense of cell contribution to the NT (Figure 2G,I,J).
evidence: Quantified from fluorescence distribution in morpholino-electroporated embryos at stages HH10-11.

claim: The average raw motility of PZ cells is higher than that of PSM or NT cells.
source: First, we noticed that the average raw motility of PZ cells is higher than that of PSM or NT cells (Figure 3C, top panel).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments tracking cell movements in 7 embryos.

claim: Raw directionality was more pronounced for PZ cells in the posterior direction compared to PSM or NT cells.
source: Raw directionality was also found more pronounced for PZ cells in the posterior direction compared to PSM or NT cells (Figure 3D, upper panel).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments analyzing cell movement directionality.

claim: PZ cells move on average as fast as PSM cells and significantly faster than NT cells (corrected motility).
source: Analysis of local (corrected) motility revealed that PZ cells move in average as fast as PSM cells and significantly faster than NT cells (Figure 3C, bottom panel).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments after tissue motion correction.

claim: Sox2high progenitor cells are less motile than Sox2-negative cells in the PZ.
source: We then compared motilities of progenitors emitting or not the eGFP fluorescent signal and found that negative cells are more motile than positive cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—video 2), thus confirming diversity in cell motile behaviors within the PZ and pointing to cells expressing Sox2 as the least motile cells.
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments using Sox2 reporter construct.

claim: The MSD of posterior progenitors is linear after tissue subtraction, as intense as the MSD of PSM cells and significantly higher than that of NT cells.
source: This analysis showed that the MSD of posterior progenitors is linear after tissue subtraction, as intense as the MSD of PSM cells and significantly higher than that of NT cells, thus demonstrating the diffusive nature of PZ cell movements (Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments analyzing mean squared displacement over time.

claim: Bra-overexpressing PZ cells display higher motility without significant differences in directionality when compared to control cells.
source: We found that Bra-overexpressing PZ cells display higher motility without significant differences in directionality when compared to control cells.
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments of electroporated embryos.

claim: When PZ cells overexpress Sox2, there is a significant reduction of their motility accompanied by an anterior bias in angle distribution compared to control cells.
source: By contrast, when PZ cells overexpress Sox2, we detected a significant reduction of their motility accompanied by an anterior bias in angle distribution compared to control cells (Figure 4B,C,D, and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments of electroporated embryos.

claim: Bra downregulation leads to significant reduction of cell motility and a change in directionality toward the anterior direction.
source: We found that Bra downregulation leads to similar significant reduction of cell motility, as well as a change in directionality toward the anterior direction (Figure 4B,E,F).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments of morpholino-electroporated embryos.

claim: Sox2 downregulation did not result in significant effect on average cell motility or directionality.
source: Conversely, Sox2 downregulation did not result in significant effect on average cell motility or directionality, even though a tendency toward a slight increase in motility was noticed (Figure 4B,E,F and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging experiments of morpholino-electroporated embryos.

claim: Neither the neural marker Pax6 nor the mesodermal marker Msgn1 is induced in PZ cells overexpressing Sox2 and Bra, respectively, 7 hours after transfection.
source: We found that neither the neural marker Pax6 nor the mesodermal marker Msgn1 was induced in PZ cells overexpressing Sox2 and Bra, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Assessed through immunodetection and in situ hybridization 7 hours after electroporation.

claim: The effects of Sox2 and Bra on PZ cell motility is not a consequence of a drastic change in the differentiation process of progenitor cells.
source: These data thus strongly support the view that the effects of Sox2 and Bra on PZ cell motility is not a consequence of a drastic change in the differentiation process of progenitor cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that differentiation markers are not induced 7 hours after Sox2/Bra overexpression.

claim: The mathematical model recapitulates the basic properties of the biological system with stable PZ cell numbers and increased NT and PSM cell numbers over time.
source: Simulations showed that the relative cell numbers (taking into account proliferation) evolve as expected with a stable number of PZ cells and an increased number of NT and PSM cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations.

claim: The mathematical model reproduces general trends with regard to cell motilities and non-directionality of cell movements.
source: We also found that this model reproduces general trends with regard to cell motilities and non-directionality of cell movements (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations.

claim: Without either random motion or adhesion/non-mixing properties, integrity of the tissues is severely affected in the model.
source: It turns out that without either random motion or adhesion/non-mixing properties, integrity of the tissues is severely affected (Figure 5F), revealing the importance of these parameters in progenitors' behavior in controlling posterior tissue morphogenesis.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations testing different parameter conditions.

claim: In the model, BraHigh values increase PZ cell motility, lead to generation of a higher number of PSM cells, to a depletion of cells in the PZ, and to a shorter NT.
source: As a result, BraHigh values increase PZ cell motility (Figure 5G), lead to generation of a higher number of PSM cells (Figure 5H), to a depletion of cells in the PZ, and to a shorter NT (Figure 5J; Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations with altered Sox2/Bra ratios.

claim: In the model, Sox2High values lead to reduced PZ cell motility, to a depletion of PZ cells, to an increased number of NT cells, and to an enlarged NT.
source: On the opposite, Sox2High values lead to reduced PZ cell motility (Figure 5G), to a depletion of PZ cells, to an increased number of NT cells, and to an enlarged NT (Figure 5I,J; Figure 5—video 2).
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations with altered Sox2/Bra ratios.

claim: The random model shows faster elongation than the gradient model, while the mixed model results in an intermediate speed.
source: We found differences between the three models, simulation of the random model showed faster elongation than simulation of the gradient model, while simulation of the mixed model resulted in an intermediate speed (Figure 6A').
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claim: Resident progenitors have traveled to a more posterior position in the random and mixed models than in the gradient model.
source: This analysis showed that resident progenitors have traveled in a more posterior position in the random and the mixed models than in the gradient model, indicating that random distribution of Sox2/Bra values is more efficient in imposing a posterior movement to these cells than graded distribution (Figure 6A'').
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations tracking resident progenitor cells.

claim: Proportions (length/width) of the PZ are much more conserved over the elongation process in the random model compared to the gradient model.
source: By analyzing the PZ shape at the beginning and at the end of the simulation, we found that proportions (length/width) of the PZ were much more conserved over the elongation process in the random model compared to the gradient model where it became larger (medio-lateral) and shorter (antero-posterior) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations analyzing tissue shape over time.

claim: The MSD of the random model is higher than that of the mixed model, which itself is higher than the MSD of the gradient model.
source: We found that the MSD of the random model is higher than that of the mixed model, which itself is higher than the MSD of the gradient model (Figure 6C), suggesting that the spatial heterogeneity in the expression of Sox2 and Bra is enhancing the diffusive behavior of PZ cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling simulations analyzing mean squared displacement.

claim: Sox2 and Bra are known to be expressed in neural progenitors and paraxial mesoderm, respectively, during embryonic development.
source: Two transcription factors, Sox2 (SRY sex-determining region Y-box 2) and Bra (Brachyury), have been described for their respective roles in neural and mesodermal specification during embryonic development (Herrmann et al., 1990; Bergsland et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Herrmann et al., 1990 and Bergsland et al., 2011.

claim: Sox2 is known to be expressed in neural progenitors that form the NT where it contributes to maintain their undifferentiated state.
source: Sox2 is known to be expressed in the neural progenitors that form the NT where it contributes to maintain their undifferentiated state.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Sox2 function in neural development.

claim: Ectopic expression of Sox2 in cells of the PSM is sufficient to reprogram these cells to adopt a neural identity.
source: Its involvement in the neural specification has also been revealed by a study showing that ectopic expression of Sox2 in cells of the PSM is sufficient to reprogram these cells, which then adopt a neural identity (Takemoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Takemoto et al., 2011.

claim: Bra protein was initially identified for its essential function in the formation of the paraxial mesoderm during the posterior extension phase.
source: Bra protein was initially identified for its essential function in the formation of the paraxial mesoderm during the posterior extension phase (Herrmann et al., 1990; Wilson et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Herrmann et al., 1990 and Wilson et al., 1995.

claim: In chimeric mouse embryos composed of both Bra mutant and wild-type cells, only wild-type cells are capable of generating posterior mesoderm.
source: Its crucial role in mesodermal specification has been demonstrated, in particular, by phenotypic study of chimeric mouse embryos composed of both Bra mutant and wild-type cells, and in which only wild-type cells are capable of generating posterior mesoderm (Wilson and Beddington, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Wilson and Beddington, 1997.

claim: Sox2 and Bra are expressed in posterior progenitors of developing embryos, indicating that activation of their expression takes place in progenitor cells before these cells colonize the NT or the PSM.
source: More recent studies have shown that Sox2 and Bra are expressed in posterior progenitors of developing embryos, indicating that activation of their expression takes place in progenitor cells before these cells colonize the NT or the PSM (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Wymeersch et al., 2016; Martin and Kimelman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012; Wymeersch et al., 2016; Martin and Kimelman, 2012.

claim: Both Sox2 and Bra proteins are co-expressed in progenitor cells.
source: In addition, these studies have shown that both proteins are co-expressed in progenitor cells, an observation consistent with the presence of bi-potent progenitors in this tissue.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies and consistent with the concept of bi-potent progenitors.

claim: Mouse progenitors display regional differences in Sox2 and Bra expression levels with regions of higher Sox2 in the PZ being neural-fated, and those with higher Bra being mesoderm-fated.
source: Importantly, it has been found that mouse progenitors display regional differences in Sox2 and Bra expression levels with regions of higher Sox2 in the PZ being neural-fated, and those with higher Bra being mesoderm-fated (Wymeersch et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Wymeersch et al., 2016.

claim: Bra and Sox2 influence the choice between neural and mesodermal lineages by their antagonistic activities on the regulation of neural and mesodermal gene expression.
source: Works done in mouse embryos and in in vitro systems derived from embryonic stem cells indicate that Bra and Sox2 influence the choice between neural and mesodermal lineages by their antagonistic activities on the regulation of neural and mesodermal gene expression (Koch et al., 2017; Veenvliet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Koch et al., 2017 and Veenvliet et al., 2020.

claim: Cells of the PZ contribute to formation of the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) and the neural tube (NT).
source: The use of fluorescent tracers in bird and mouse embryos has revealed that cells of the PZ, called here posterior progenitors, contribute to formation of the presomitic mesoderm (PSM), the mesodermal tissue that generates muscle and vertebrae but also of the neural tube (NT), the neuro-ectodermal tissue that gives rise to the central nervous system (Selleck and Stern, 1991; Iimura et al., 2007; Wilson and Beddington, 1996; Psychoyos and Stern, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies using fluorescent tracers in bird and mouse embryos.

claim: Resident posterior progenitors have the capacity to self-renew while providing new neural and mesodermal progenies.
source: Grafting experiments next showed that resident posterior progenitors have the capacity to self-renew while providing new neural and mesodermal progenies (Cambray and Wilson, 2002; McGrew et al., 2008), thus indicating that the PZ contains progenitors of different tissues.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous grafting experiments by Cambray and Wilson, 2002 and McGrew et al., 2008.

claim: Retrospective clonal analysis studies in mouse embryo revealed the existence of single progenitors giving rise either to neural or mesodermal cells, and bi-potent progenitors (NMPs) that generate both neural and mesodermal cells.
source: Heterogeneity in the progeny of PZ cells was further confirmed by retrospective clonal analysis studies performed in the mouse embryo which revealed the existence of single progenitors, giving rise either to neural or mesodermal cells, but also of bi-potent progenitors, named neuro-mesodermal progenitors (NMPs), that generate both neural and mesodermal cells (Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous clonal analysis study by Tzouanacou et al., 2009.

claim: The existence of bi-potent progenitors has been shown at earlier stages of zebrafish development and in bird embryos.
source: The existence of bi-potent progenitors has since been shown at earlier stages of zebrafish development (Attardi et al., 2018) and in bird embryos (Solovieva et al., 2020; Wood et al., 2019; Guillot et al., 2021) (for reviews Wymeersch et al., 2021; Sambasivan and Steventon, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in zebrafish and bird embryos.

claim: High levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT.
source: Our data support a model in which high levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT while high levels of Bra rather give them high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from overexpression and time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: High levels of Bra give cells high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
source: Our data support a model in which high levels of Sox2 give cells low motile properties and make them integrate the NT while high levels of Bra rather give them high motile and diffusive properties that push them to exit the PZ and integrate the PSM.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from overexpression and time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Progenitors co-expressing Sox2 and Bra at comparable levels move with an intermediate speed and remain resident of the PZ as this tissue is moving posteriorly.
source: Located in-between these low and high motile/diffusive cells are progenitors co-expressing Sox2 and Bra at comparable levels, that are moving with an intermediate speed and remain resident of the PZ as this tissue is moving posteriorly.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing different motility levels based on Sox2/Bra ratios.

claim: While graded expression of Sox2/Bra confers a higher short-term stability in PZ shape, random distribution provides a higher rate of elongation, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
source: Indeed, while graded expression of Sox2/Bra confers a higher short-term stability in PZ shape, random distribution provides a higher rate of elongation, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claim: The gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations.
source: Taken together, by exploring and comparing Sox2/Bra spatial distributions, our modeling data indicate that while the gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations, random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claim: Random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
source: Taken together, by exploring and comparing Sox2/Bra spatial distributions, our modeling data indicate that while the gradient pattern provides stability by limiting local and transient deformations, random distribution of cell-to-cell heterogeneity could promote cell rearrangements, tissue fluidity, and long-term conservation of tissue shape.
evidence: Demonstrated through mathematical modeling comparing different spatial distribution patterns.

claim: Brachyury plays a role in cell migration.
source: It has been shown that Brachyury plays a role in cell migration (Wilson et al., 1995; Wilson and Beddington, 1997; Turner et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Brachyury function.

claim: Mouse cells that have a mutation in the Brachyury gene have lower migration speed than wild-type cells when isolated and cultured.
source: In particular, mouse cells that have a mutation in the Brachyury gene have lower migration speed than wild-type cells when isolated and cultured, explaining part of the mouse embryonic axis truncation phenotype (Hashimoto et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Hashimoto et al., 1987.

claim: A rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation.
source: Although a role for Sox2 in the control of progenitor cell migration has, to our knowledge, not previously been reported, recent works have demonstrated that a rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation (Kawachi et al., 2020) and that turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo (Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Kawachi et al., 2020.

claim: Turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo.
source: Although a role for Sox2 in the control of progenitor cell migration has, to our knowledge, not previously been reported, recent works have demonstrated that a rise of Sox2 expression promotes the transition of posterior progenitors to NT during chick embryo secondary neurulation (Kawachi et al., 2020) and that turning off Sox2 is necessary for NMP to enter the mesoderm in zebrafish embryo (Kinney et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Kinney et al., 2020.

claim: The dorsal zone between the PZ and the NT does not display excessive cell migration but rather local cell intercalations.
source: In addition, it has also been observed by time-lapse analysis that the dorsal zone between the PZ and the NT does not display excessive cell migration but rather local cell intercalations (Roszko et al., 2007; Gonzalez-Gobartt et al., 2021a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous time-lapse studies by Roszko et al., 2007 and Gonzalez-Gobartt et al., 2021a.

claim: Posterior progenitors undergo an epithelial-mesenchymal transition before reaching their full potential to give rise to progeny in the NT and the PSM.
source: In line with this explanation is the fact that during the course of axis elongation posterior progenitors undergo an epithelial-mesenchymal transition before reaching their full potential to give rise to progeny in the NT and the PSM (Guillot et al., 2021; Goto et al., 2017; Dias et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Guillot et al., 2021; Goto et al., 2017; Dias et al., 2020.

claim: Physical constraints exerted by neighboring tissues, in particular the PSM, promote the posterior movement of the PZ.
source: Several works, performed in bird embryo, have indicated that physical constraints exerted by neighboring tissues, in particular the PSM, promote the posterior movement of the PZ (Bénazéraf et al., 2017; Bénazéraf et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2020; Regev et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on physical constraints in bird embryos.

claim: Differential adhesion between progenitors could regulate their segregation.
source: One interesting possibility that is taken into account in our mathematical models is that, as it has been demonstrated during NT dorso-ventral patterning (Tsai et al., 2020), differential adhesion between progenitors could regulate their segregation.
evidence: Speculative possibility based on previous work by Tsai et al., 2020 on differential adhesion in NT patterning.

claim: Fluid-like state and disordered cellular movements have been described in PSM tissue to be key for zebrafish embryo axis elongation and morphogenesis.
source: Interestingly, this fluid-like state as well as disordered cellular movements have been described in PSM tissue to be key for zebrafish embryo axis elongation and morphogenesis (Lawton et al., 2013; Das et al., 2017; Mongera et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on PSM tissue properties in zebrafish.

claim: The PZ is able to regenerate after partial ablation.
source: Several studies have shown that this particular region of the embryo is able to regenerate after partial ablation (Joubin and Stern, 1999; Yuan and Schoenwolf, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous ablation studies by Joubin and Stern, 1999 and Yuan and Schoenwolf, 1999.

claim: Spatial cell-to-cell heterogeneity appears to be an enabling factor for self-correction in the PZ.
source: Spatial cell-to-cell heterogeneity, which allows easier re-organization of remaining cells than graded cell pattern, thus appears to be an enabling factor for self-correction.
evidence: Inferred from modeling results showing better shape conservation with random distribution.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity in gene and protein expression is a common trait of living systems and has been observed in many contexts including early mouse embryos or cancer cells.
source: Spatial heterogeneity in gene and protein expression is a common trait of living systems and has been observed in many contexts including, early mouse embryos or cancer cells (Prasetyanti and Medema, 2017; Fiorentino et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on cellular heterogeneity in different biological contexts.
